profiles.meeting_scenario: Two ML researchers are holding a brainstorming meeting to generate a workshop-style project idea in computational psychiatry after reading a review on neural network models of schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder. Their lab has a 6-week exploratory window and access to existing embodied-agent code, lightweight simulators, and prior recurrent-model tooling, but no capacity for a full new dataset or clinical collaboration. The agenda is to identify a novel direction that responds to the review's critique of overly narrow symptom-specific models, especially by considering sensorimotor integration and body perception, and to narrow the discussion to one candidate concept they can pitch internally. The expected outcome is loose alignment on a project framing, a rough prototype direction, and an informal split of next-step drafting work.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Computational psychiatry, predictive processing, mechanistic neural-network modeling
members.background: Maya leads a small academic lab studying neural-network models of psychiatric symptoms, with prior work on recurrent perception-action loops, Bayesian brain accounts, and theory-driven simulation papers that connect latent mechanisms to behavioral signatures.
members.private_state: She wants a concept that sounds intellectually coherent and genuinely broader than past one-symptom toy models, but that can still be illustrated quickly without committing the lab to a full empirical benchmark effort.
hidden_assumptions: A 'shared framework' means one mechanistic model family whose disorder differences come from parameter regimes or internal perturbations, not separately engineered solutions under one repo.
An 'embodied setup' naturally implies a closed-loop agent whose actions update future sensory evidence and body-state beliefs online.
A 'minimal prototype' can be a compelling demonstration even if learning is mostly bypassed, as long as one simulated trajectory or controlled parameter sweep makes the mechanism legible.

Being 'grounded in the review' means extracting its theoretical lesson that existing models are too narrow and then building around principles like precision weighting, predictive coding, or free-energy style body-state inference.

members.name: Arjun Patel
members.expertise: Deep learning experimentation, embodied ML, reproducible training pipelines
members.background: Arjun is a senior PhD student who builds PyTorch agents for multimodal and embodied tasks, with strong instincts for using existing simulators, standard training loops, and interpretable experimental scaffolds that can turn into figures quickly.
members.private_state: He wants a direction that can become an end-to-end working experiment rather than a mostly conceptual simulation, and he prefers to anchor novelty in a clean empirical setup built from modern ML components he can execute fast.
hidden_assumptions: A 'shared framework' can still include separate condition-specific heads, perturbation modules, or training runs, as long as the implementation and evaluation pipeline are unified.

An 'embodied setup' naturally includes standard simulator rollouts, logged trajectories, and action-conditioned observations even if the first pass is mostly offline or replay-based rather than actively interactive.
A 'minimal prototype' should still be a trainable end-to-end system that successfully learns the toy task, even if it uses only one environment, one architecture family, and light analysis.

Being 'grounded in the review' means taking the salient symptom patterns and failure modes it highlights—such as detail fixation, hallucination-like misperception, or altered sensory precision—and operationalizing them as perturbations or evaluation probes on a modern architecture.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to look for a 'shared framework' for ASD and schizophrenia.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a single mechanistic architecture or model family in which both disorders emerge from changing a small set of internal assumptions or parameters, such as precision weighting or inhibitory balance.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means one common project scaffold—shared codebase, simulator, and evaluation pipeline—even if ASD-like and schizophrenia-like effects are implemented through partially different modules, heads, or training conditions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In an early brainstorming meeting, 'shared framework' sounds like obvious agreement because both are contrasting against doing two unrelated projects; the phrase is abstract enough that theoretical unity and engineering unity pass as the same thing.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the idea should use an 'embodied setup' to move beyond static symptom models.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes online action-perception coupling, body-state estimation, and closed-loop updating where the agent's interventions alter what it senses next.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes visually or proprioceptively grounded trajectories in a simulator, but assumes the first prototype can rely on replayed episodes or logged rollouts with action-conditioned inputs rather than true closed-loop interaction.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both associate 'embodied' with agents, actions, and multimodal signals, so the overlap feels strong; the difference between closed-loop embodiment and replay-based embodied data hides inside what each sees as an implementation detail, not a conceptual mismatch.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to start with a 'minimal prototype' during the 6-week window.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks a minimal prototype could be a lightly engineered demonstration—such as a controlled recurrent model, a hand-tuned perturbation, or even a few illustrative simulated trajectories—that makes the mechanistic claim visible without full training.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks a minimal prototype still needs an actual end-to-end training run that converges on a small toy task, because otherwise it is not yet a real ML prototype.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'minimal prototype' routinely signals pragmatism to both of them, but each silently calibrates it to their own craft norms: conceptual proof for M1 versus trainable system for M2.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the project should be 'grounded in the review.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes that grounding in the review means extracting its theoretical through-line—especially predictive-processing, free-energy, precision, and dysconnection ideas—and using those principles to shape the architecture or latent variables.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes that grounding in the review means extracting the symptom patterns and behavioral signatures it surveys, then building a modern embodied model and testing whether those signatures appear under controlled perturbations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both literally read the same paper and invoke it as common context, each assumes the relevant takeaway is self-evident; 'grounded in the review' sounds fully shared even though one is taking away design principles and the other is taking away evaluation targets.

turns.inner_thought: The review's main weakness critique is that people build isolated toy accounts for single symptoms and then imply broad relevance. What I want is one mechanistic model family where ASD-like and schizophrenia-like phenomena fall out from changing a compact set of internal assumptions—precision, gain, maybe inhibitory balance—not two separate engineered solutions under one project banner. And if we say it's grounded in the review, to me that means carrying forward the predictive-processing through-line, especially around body-state inference and dysregulated precision.
turns.utterance: One thing that really stayed with me from the review is its complaint that the field keeps carving things into very narrow symptom models. Do you think we could sketch a shared framework that says something about both ASD and schizophrenia, while still being grounded in the review?

turns.inner_thought: Yes, this is promising if I keep it executable. For me, shared framework means one project scaffold—same codebase, simulator, training and eval flow—even if the disorder cases end up using somewhat different perturbations or conditions. Grounded in the review should mean we preserve the salient symptom patterns and failure modes it highlights. And if we lean on the embodied-agent tooling I already have, we can make this real quickly.
turns.utterance: Yeah, definitely. That would be exciting if it stays tied to the paper but still fits something we can build quickly with a modern embodied pipeline.

turns.inner_thought: The cleanest concept is a closed-loop agent continuously inferring its own body state while acting, so its interventions change the incoming sensory evidence and the next inference step. Then altered precision or inhibitory balance can yield different behavioral signatures without changing the basic architecture. That's a principled answer to the review's critique, and it keeps the project conceptually anchored in predictive processing rather than generic RL.
turns.utterance: One framing I like is to center it on an embodied setup where altered precision or inhibitory balance changes how the agent tracks its own body state while acting. That feels like a good way to move beyond the static symptom stories the review was pushing against.

turns.inner_thought: This should be feasible because I already have simulator rollouts, action-conditioned observations, and multimodal streams from earlier embodied work. For a first pass, I can seed things from logged trajectories rather than requiring fully interactive control from day one and still have something clearly embodied. If it works, tightening the loop later is straightforward.
turns.utterance: I think that part is pretty doable on our end. I already have simulator trajectories and action-conditioned observation streams from earlier code, so we could use those to seed a first version instead of building everything from scratch.

turns.inner_thought: The elegant version is one architecture, one generative story, and the disorder contrast appears by dialing a few internal parameters. If hallucination-like instability and autism-like detail fixation can both emerge as nearby regimes of the same model family, that's exactly the conceptual win I want for an internal pitch.
turns.utterance: And conceptually, it would be especially elegant if the same model could express hallucination-like instability and autism-like detail fixation just by shifting a few internal settings within that shared framework.

turns.inner_thought: I can support that at the project level by keeping one core implementation and applying different disorder-related perturbations or conditions. To me that's still unified because the simulator, architecture family, logging, and evaluation story are shared. As long as it doesn't turn into two disconnected projects, we're fine.
turns.utterance: Yeah, totally. We can keep one core implementation and just apply the different condition perturbations, which should still give us a clean overall story.

turns.inner_thought: I need to protect scope. In six weeks, I do not want us getting trapped in infrastructure or benchmark ambitions. A minimal prototype, to me, could just be a compact recurrent simulation, maybe partly hand-tuned, with a couple of illustrative trajectories or a small sweep that makes the mechanism obvious. If the mechanism is legible, that's enough for the lab pitch.
turns.utterance: Given the six-week window, I think we should be strict about what counts as success. For a minimal prototype, even a compact simulation with a couple of illustrative trajectories could be enough if it cleanly shows the mechanism.

turns.inner_thought: Minimal prototype is fine, but I still interpret that as something that actually runs as a learned system on a toy embodied task. Otherwise we'll just have a concept sketch. I think I can get a small trainable version working and use that to generate trajectories, figures, and some basic probes within six weeks if I reuse existing assets.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable. I think I can get a basic version running on one toy task within the window, which would at least give us something concrete to look at and generate those trajectories.

turns.inner_thought: I should make sure we don't drift into generic embodied ML with psychiatric labels pasted on afterward. Grounded in the review, for me, means the architecture and perturbation logic should inherit predictive-processing and free-energy intuitions from the start—especially precision weighting and body-state inference. Otherwise the whole thing will feel superficial.
turns.utterance: The one thing I want to protect is that it should really be grounded in the review in a substantive way. I'd rather it inherit that predictive-processing and free-energy intuition than just bolt psychiatric labels onto a standard agent.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed, and the practical upside of the review is that it gives us concrete signatures to test once the model is trained—detail over-attention, misperceiving self-generated signals, altered sensitivity patterns. That's what will make the project feel empirically anchored rather than just themed around psychiatry.
turns.utterance: Yeah, I agree. The nice thing is that the paper also gives us some concrete signatures to probe—like over-attending to details or misperceiving generated signals—once the agent is up and running.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then I'll shape the pitch around one mechanistic story and disorder-specific parameter regimes, and let him flesh out the embodied side. I assume his setup will naturally include the closed-loop body-state piece I have in mind. If I keep the note at the right level, we can sound broader than our old toy models without committing to a huge empirical benchmark.
turns.utterance: Maybe the clean next step is: you sketch the embodied setup in enough detail that we can see the task and signals, and I'll draft the concept note around one mechanistic story with disorder-specific parameter regimes. Then we can combine them into a pitch.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll outline a prototype around the simulator assets I already have, keep it scoped to something executable, and add a few review-inspired probes so the evaluation looks crisp. That should give us a solid internal note quickly, even if the first version is lightweight.
